vacancies.text: District 10 is vacant: Ali Brown resigned September 10, 2026 to lead the Indiana Alliance of Boys and Girls Clubs. The Marion County Democratic Party is to choose a successor at a caucus by October 10.

questions.statement: City government should have a dedicated office focused on equity and inclusion.
questions.text: Confirm the Mayor's appointment of Benjamin Tapper as Director of the Office of Equity, Belonging and Inclusion.

since.t: The Office of Equity, Belonging and Inclusion leads the city's DEI work through data reporting, training (on request) and community programming. It was created with $687,865 set aside in the 2024 budget.

questions.statement: Cities should use tax revenue from designated zones to help fund professional sports facilities.
questions.text: Approve an additional Professional Sports Development Area.

since.t: The area was created for a potential Major League Soccer stadium. The Metropolitan Development Commission later confirmed (6–1) a stadium development district at the downtown heliport site.

As of September 2026 the city has not secured an MLS team; talks resumed in September and now point to a site near Lucas Oil Stadium. The separate Eleven Park stadium's construction was in doubt after the city withdrew financial support.

questions.statement: Changing traffic laws to make public transit easier is important to me.
questions.text: Authorize traffic control changes to the city code in support of an IndyGo public transportation project.

since.t: Related results: IndyGo's Purple Line has had the highest monthly ridership of any IndyGo route since November 2024. The earlier Red Line has run below its projected 11,000 trips a day after three years of operation.

questions.statement: Special economic districts are a good tool for supporting growth in business areas.
questions.text: Replace the Mile Square Economic Enhancement District with a new Economic Enhancement District chapter.
questions.context: Economic Enhancement Districts let a city levy an added assessment on property owners inside a defined area. Downtown Indianapolis's "Mile Square" district, as proposed, charges businesses and apartment buildings 0.1681% of assessed value and homeowners a flat $250, raising about $5.5M a year for cleaning crews, public safety ambassadors and homeless outreach. The state authorized this kind of district in 2023 and the Council created the Mile Square district that December; the state House then moved to repeal it, but lawmakers ultimately advanced changes that preserved it. This vote replaced the original city chapter with a new Economic Enhancement District chapter.

since.t: Downtown Indy, Inc.'s plan put about $1.9M toward 28 cleaning ambassadors and four supervisors, supplies, restrooms on Monument Circle and beautification, and about $450,000 toward public safety (extra off-duty bike patrols and non-police safety ambassadors). The sources reviewed did not include published results on how well the district has worked.
Critics' objection was the funding mechanism: a House committee voted 15–9, largely along party lines, to repeal the district's state authorization in January 2024.

questions.statement: Indianapolis should adopt a formal goal of eliminating traffic deaths and injuries.
questions.text: Commit to eliminating traffic injuries and fatalities and create a Vision Zero Task Force and Action Plan.

since.t: The Vision Zero Task Force, formed in August 2024, later adopted a 102-page action plan built around safe speeds, streets, people, vehicles and post-crash care, with a goal of eliminating traffic deaths and serious injuries by 2035.
The city's first Vision Zero report counted 85 traffic deaths in 2025, down from more than 120 at the 2021 pandemic-era peak; pedestrians and cyclists made up over 30%.
Some advocates say progress is too slow, and city officials acknowledge long-term funding for quick-build safety projects is a challenge.

questions.statement: The mayor and elected county officials like the auditor, clerk and assessor deserve a pay raise after years without one.
questions.text: Raise pay for countywide elected offices (auditor, clerk, assessor and others) now and for the mayor starting with the next term.

since.t: Mayor Hogsett said he would veto any pay package that raised his own pay mid-term. The final version raised the mayor's salary from $95,000 to $125,000 (the first raise since 2002) only from January 1, 2028, the start of the next term. Countywide offices such as auditor, clerk and assessor, flat since 2010, were raised to roughly $92,000.
Opponents of the final version argued raises shouldn't take effect mid-term; a Republican amendment to delay them to each official's next term failed 6–18.

questions.statement: Road and bridge repair should be funded first, even if it means cutting other city departments' budgets.
questions.text: Direct the city controller to revise the 2025 budget to add road and bridge repair funding by reducing other departments' budgets.

since.t: The state later created a road-funding program that requires a growing local match ($50M in 2027, rising to $100M by 2031). The city's 2027 proposed budget reflects it, with roads, bridges and greenways rising to $267M.

src.label: City budget books (summarized by Indy AI Research Docs)

questions.statement: Public transit deserves continued local tax funding.
questions.text: Adopt IndyGo's 2025 operating budget and tax levy.

since.t: Related results: the Purple Line passed 100,000 monthly riders in April 2025 and has been IndyGo's busiest route since November 2024; the Red Line's ridership has stayed below its 11,000-a-day projection.

questions.statement: Local officials should push to lower local tax rates whenever the state allows it.
questions.text: Ask the state to approve a lower levy freeze tax rate for Marion County.

since.t: Separately, the state's 2025 property tax overhaul (Senate Enrolled Act 1) repeals the levy freeze rate, and the city told councilors it left a roughly $43M revenue hole that the 2026 budget had to close, partly with higher permit fees.

questions.statement: City employees should not be required to live in Marion County.
questions.text: Loosen the requirement that city employees live in Marion County.

since.t: The Council rejected the change, but the push moved to the state: a 2026 bill (HB 1025) would bar county residency requirements for public defenders and their staff, motivated by hard-to-fill Marion County public defender vacancies.
The 50-year-old city residency rule remains for other city employees.

questions.statement: The police chief, not a civilian-majority board, should have the final say on police department policies.
questions.text: Make the General Orders Board advisory only, giving the police chief final authority over IMPD general orders.

since.t: The General Orders Board was created in 2020 after civil unrest and local use-of-force controversies, and can approve IMPD conduct policies. Sponsors said the change would give the chief "agility"; the Fraternal Order of Police said policy changes face 45 overlapping levels of review.
The Council rejected the change, but state lawmakers took it up in 2026 (Senate Bill 284), which would make civilian general-orders boards advisory statewide; it advanced out of committee.

questions.statement: The city should fund community development and crime-prevention grants to neighborhood organizations.
questions.text: Approve the 2026 budget's community development grants and crime prevention (Elevate) grants.
questions.context: The 2026 budget passed 17–8, but the Council voted separately on eight sections so members with conflicts (for example nonprofit jobs) could abstain. This one covers community development grants and crime prevention (Elevate) grants to neighborhood organizations.

since.t: Murders in Indianapolis fell to 133 in 2025, down about 45% from the 2021 record of 241, by IMPD figures reported by WFYI (other outlets count homicides slightly differently). Coverage credits several factors, including police strategy, technology and a crime-guns task force, alongside community violence-reduction programs, and doesn't isolate how much any one program contributed.
A 2026 city audit of the Office of Public Health and Safety, which runs these grant programs, found weak contract oversight (see the public-health-and-safety question).

questions.statement: The city is funding economic development and housing (Department of Metropolitan Development) at about the right level.
questions.text: Approve the 2026 budget's appropriations for the Department of Metropolitan Development.
questions.context: The Department of Metropolitan Development (DMD) handles planning, zoning, historic preservation and housing and community development. Most of its budget is federal housing and community-development money that it passes through to developers and nonprofits. In the city's budget books it totals about $45.6M (2024 actual), $55.5M (2025 actual) and $90.3M (2026 adopted), of which roughly $74M in 2026 is federal grants.

since.t: The mayor's proposed 2027 budget raises DMD to about $105.8M. Housing initiatives across DMD, OPHS and other agencies total about $72M, including $2.7M to run a 150-bed low-barrier shelter (the "Housing Hub") that is planned to open in summer 2027.

src.label: City budget books (summarized by Indy AI Research Docs)

since.t: DMD's growth since 2024 comes mostly from federal pass-through grants rather than local tax dollars.

src.label: City budget books (summarized by Indy AI Research Docs)

questions.statement: The city is funding streets, bridges and public works at about the right level.
questions.text: Approve the 2026 budget's appropriations for the Department of Public Works.
questions.context: The Department of Public Works handles roads, bridges, sidewalks, trails and stormwater; potholes, snow removal and street sweeping; trash and recycling; the city vehicle fleet; traffic signals; and Vision Zero safety work. Across all funds its budget was about $250.8M (2024 actual), $260.9M (2025 actual) and $257.4M (2026 adopted), so 2026 was roughly flat to slightly down.

since.t: The mayor's proposed 2027 budget raises Public Works to about $335M, driven by the new state road program ($50M from the state, contingent on a local match). Its Vision Zero work includes a Quick Build program for fast, low-cost fixes at dangerous intersections and a Fatal Crash Review Team.

src.label: City budget books (summarized by Indy AI Research Docs)

questions.statement: The city is funding public health and violence-prevention programs (Office of Public Health and Safety) at about the right level.
questions.text: Approve the 2026 budget's appropriations for the Office of Public Health and Safety.
questions.context: The Office of Public Health and Safety (OPHS) runs the city's non-police public safety work: violence reduction (Indy Peace and Elevation Grants), homelessness and eviction prevention, a clinician-led crisis response team dispatched through 911, reentry and food policy. Most of its money goes out as grants and contracts to community groups. Its budget was about $25.3M (2024 actual), $31.2M (2025 actual) and $28.0M (2026 adopted).

since.t: A 2026 city audit found OPHS lacked proper oversight of its programs and finances, with eight "high risk" findings and missing or incomplete documentation on 84% of contracts reviewed. OPHS said it is writing procedures and building public dashboards.
The clinician crisis team now covers all of Marion County (May 2026), and a new agreement with 911 aims to route more behavioral health calls to clinicians instead of police.

questions.statement: The city should shift money from violence-prevention (Elevate) grants to preserving urban forests.
questions.text: Amend the 2026 budget to move funding from crime prevention grants toward urban forest preservation.

since.t: Residents and the Indiana Forest Alliance pressed for a $3M urban forest acquisition fund, citing Marion County tree canopy that fell from about 32% (2014) to about 27%.

In debate, supporters of the amendment said the budget should fund forests; opponents said the Elevate grants fund roughly 200 organizations and a drop in homicides, and some who opposed it (including Councilor J. Brown) said they support forest funding but not at the grants' expense. Councilors noted about $1M was secured for forest preservation earlier in 2025 and about $4M in stormwater money was held for a future Urban Forest Preservation Fund.

questions.statement: The city should keep funding police positions even when the department can't fill them.
questions.context: IMPD's 2025 union contract funds 1,437 officers, but a councilor said in December 2025 the department was down to about 1,300. Another councilor said in October 2025 that the 2026 budget funds "more than 300" officers the department doesn't have. (Figures are as stated in Council meeting minutes, not independently verified.)

since.t: The city's budget books say the 2026 budget funds 1,743 IMPD officer positions, with about 1,383 filled (roughly 360 vacant).

src.label: City budget books (summarized by Indy AI Research Docs)

questions.statement: Data center developers should be pressured to listen to community concerns before building.
questions.text: Pass a resolution urging data center developers to heed community voices.

since.t: Council-led forums found data centers among residents' top concerns.

In August 2026 the Council adopted, 23–1, the city's first data center zoning rules (a new special-use district): a noise cap, a 200-foot buffer from residential land, limits on backup-generator testing, proof of power and water capacity and annual reporting. The Council also advanced a pause on new data center permits until at least the end of 2027, sending it to the Metropolitan Development Commission for final approval.

questions.statement: Elected officials' home addresses should be kept off public disclosure forms.
questions.text: Remove the home address from the Councilor Disclosure Statement.

since.t: The proposal followed a targeted incident involving a councilor's home; supporters said public addresses on disclosure forms created a safety risk.
The Council adopted the change in June 2026.

questions.statement: The city should invest more in oversight and expansion of charter schools.
questions.text: Appropriate $276,809 to expand charter school authorizing work at the Office of Education Innovation.

since.t: The Office of Education Innovation authorizes mayor-sponsored charter schools: about 45 schools serving over 19,000 students. The appropriation is for expanded authorizing work and software modernization, funded from state grants and the charter school sub-fund.
Authorizing rules inside Indianapolis Public Schools boundaries changed in April 2026. In one case, a charter school facing scrutiny from its authorizer was approved by a different one.

questions.statement: Teenagers up to age 17 should be subject to the city's public safety curfew hours.
questions.text: Apply the Public Safety curfew hours to anyone seventeen years of age and younger.

since.t: The Council had already updated the curfew in 2025: standard hours for ages 15–17 are 11 p.m.–5 a.m. Sunday–Thursday and 1 a.m.–5 a.m. weekends; when a "Public Safety Curfew" is declared, ages 15–16 must be off the streets by 9 p.m. Sunday–Thursday. Parents get a written notice for a first offense, then fines of $500 and $1,500.
The sources reviewed did not include an evaluation of whether the curfew changed youth violence.

questions.statement: The Council should require the Office of Public Health and Safety to change how it operates based on audit findings.
questions.text: Direct the city-county to require changes to the Office of Public Health and Safety following an audit.
questions.context: In April 2026 the city's Office of Audit and Performance reported eight "high risk" findings at the Office of Public Health and Safety, including missing or incomplete documentation for 84% of the contracts it reviewed, and a $75,000 grant with a perceived conflict of interest. OPHS's budget grew about 75% from 2020 to 2025, to over $33M. OPHS said it was already writing procedures, building public dashboards and expanding procurement and ethics training. This resolution, sponsored by Councilor Hart, would have had the Council direct required changes.

since.t: The resolution failed 6–18. OPHS's 2027 budget priorities include finishing its response to the audit and reviving a database to measure program impact.

questions.statement: Raising vehicle registration taxes is a reasonable way to pay for road repair.
questions.text: Raise the county excise and wheel taxes to create dedicated road funding.

since.t: The Council passed it 14–10, Mayor Hogsett vetoed it (citing household budgets), and the Council overrode the veto 17–7 on August 10, 2026.

Most vehicles will pay a flat $100 a year (up from roughly $7.50–$20 now) and heavy vehicles a $240 wheel tax, effective 2027. The city projects about $71M in new revenue in 2027 and roughly $356M over five years, which lets it claim state road money: a $50M match in 2027 that grows to $100M a year by 2031.

questions.statement: Indianapolis should stop building new jails and detention facilities for decades.
questions.text: Urge a 40-year moratorium on building new jails after the Criminal Justice Campus is completed.

since.t: The Community Justice Campus, which replaced several older jails with one purpose-built facility with capacity for about 3,000 people, opened in 2022 at a cost of roughly $575M. The 2021 resolution was non-binding.

questions.statement: Cities should legally protect people experiencing homelessness from discrimination and arbitrary treatment.
questions.text: Amend the city code's protections for the homeless.

since.t: The 2021 amendments to the city's "Homeless Bill of Rights" require 15 days' notice before the city clears an encampment and storage of belongings for at least 60 days, while letting the Office of Public Health and Safety close camps that pose health or safety risks or when shelter space is available.
The city's 2027 budget proposal includes about $2.7M to operate a planned 150-bed low-barrier shelter, the first publicly built shelter in Indianapolis.

src.label: City budget books (summarized by Indy AI Research Docs)

questions.statement: Government should cap the fees delivery apps charge restaurants during a public health emergency.
questions.text: Temporarily limit fees third-party delivery services can charge restaurants during the COVID-19 pandemic.

since.t: The cap was temporary, tied to the COVID-19 pandemic: delivery and other fees limited to 20% of a meal's price, with apps barred from passing the lost fees on to customers or drivers. No Indianapolis-specific results were found.

questions.statement: Local public health orders should stay in effect even after the state ends its emergency declaration.
questions.text: Keep COVID-19 public health orders valid after the governor's disaster emergency expires.

since.t: The ordinance kept the Marion County health director's COVID-19 orders valid after the governor's disaster emergency ended. The sources reviewed did not include an assessment of its effect.

questions.statement: Smoking should be banned in public parks.
questions.text: Expand nonsmoking areas to include public parks owned or leased by the city or county.

since.t: The ban, which includes e-cigarettes, took effect July 1, 2021. First offenses get a $100 ticket from park rangers; later violations can mean fines of $200 to $7,500. Supporters of the measure said signs and awareness work better than fines. No enforcement totals were found in the sources reviewed.

questions.statement: The city should pay for legal help for immigrants, asylum seekers and people facing deportation.
questions.text: Appropriate $100,000 to pilot a legal protection fund for residents seeking asylum, citizenship or facing deportation.

since.t: The Indianapolis Immigrant Legal Services Fund, administered with The Indianapolis Foundation, has mobilized over $1.5M for legal services, with grants of $50,000 to $100,000 to nonprofit providers for work such as naturalization, work authorization and deportation defense.

questions.statement: Public tax-increment financing is a good way to support private redevelopment projects.
questions.text: Approve tax-increment bonds (up to $12.3 million) for the Stutz Factory mixed-use redevelopment.

since.t: The developer, SomeraRoad, invested about $100M in the Stutz building (a 441,000-square-foot, seven-building complex) and reopened it in summer 2023; the Council approved a $12.3M developer-backed tax-increment bond for it. A 52,000-square-foot lease with manufacturer Calumet was announced in January 2024.

questions.statement: Property tax breaks for developers are a good way to get affordable housing built.
questions.text: Approve a payment-in-lieu-of-taxes arrangement for a tax-credit affordable housing project.

since.t: The ordinance covers a low-income-housing-tax-credit project: state law exempts such projects from property tax, and the payment-in-lieu-of-taxes (PILOT) sets what the owner pays instead. The sources reviewed did not include a report on how this project performed.

questions.statement: The Council should publicly support protecting reproductive rights.
questions.text: Express support for the protection of reproductive rights.

since.t: This was a non-binding resolution: it states the Council's position but doesn't change any local rule or law.

questions.statement: The city should create dedicated funding to protect and grow tree canopy.
questions.text: Support mechanisms to protect and generate revenue for maintaining urban forests and trees.

since.t: Marion County's tree canopy has fallen from about 32% (2014) to about 27%, according to the Indiana Forest Alliance; advocates continue to press for a dedicated acquisition fund. The 2022 resolution was non-binding.

questions.statement: The city should use public bonds to help build a convention center hotel.
questions.text: Approve up to $625 million in bonds for a convention center headquarters hotel at Pan Am Plaza.

since.t: The bonds financed an 800-room convention-center-connected hotel at Pan Am Plaza (now the Signia by Hilton) alongside a $250M convention center expansion; both are scheduled to open in fall 2026, with construction reported ahead of schedule.
The hotel's projected cost rose about $70M, to roughly $571M, above the original $501M maximum; the Capital Improvement Board is covering the increase.

questions.statement: Local governments should have the power to pass their own gun safety rules.
questions.text: Add gun safety measures to city code, taking effect only if state limits on local regulation are repealed.

since.t: Indiana's Attorney General called the ordinance unconstitutional and "a meaningless and futile gesture," since state law preempts most local gun rules. Mayor Hogsett's office said that opinion isn't binding but acknowledged the measures can't be enforced unless the state repeals the preemption law.

questions.statement: Short-term rentals like Airbnb should be required to have a city permit.
questions.text: Create the Indianapolis Short-Term Rental Permit Program.

since.t: The permit program began in 2025 with a one-time $150 fee. By the city's mid-2025 count, 137 properties had permits and about 15 violations had been issued, with no permits revoked, while thousands of listings were still online.
